entities.summary:
The Battle of the Allia was a pivotal clash between the Gauls and the Roman Republic, taking place on July 18, 390 BCE, near the Allia River in what is now Italy. This brutal conflict marked a turning point in Roman history as the Gauls, led by Brennus, breached the Roman defenses and pillaged the city.

The Roman Republic, still in its formative years, suffered a crushing defeat, with estimates suggesting that up to 6,000 Roman soldiers perished. The Gauls, known for their ferocity and skill in battle, had long been a thorn in the side of the Romans, and their victory at the Allia River only emboldened their ambitions.

The aftermath of the battle saw the Romans regroup and reorganize their forces, but the sting of defeat would be felt for generations to come. The legacy of the Battle of the Allia serves as a stark reminder of the fragility of power and the importance of strategic alliances in the face of external threats.

As the Roman historian Livy noted, 'The calamity of the Allia was a wound that would not heal, a reminder that even the greatest of civilizations can fall victim to the whims of fate.'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Battle of the Allia had a lasting impact on Roman foreign policy, contributing to a greater emphasis on military preparedness and strategic alliances. The defeat at the Allia River also had a profound effect on the Roman psyche, contributing to a growing sense of insecurity and vulnerability.
